description: Christian teaching on raising children to believe in God and the indoctrination counter-argument.
content_html:
What Is Religious Upbringing?

Religious upbringing refers to the process of raising a child within a faith community. For Christians, this typically involves baptism or dedication as an infant, regular prayer at home, church attendance, Sunday school or youth groups, Christian festivals, and where available, faith schools. The sum of these practices creates an environment in which Christian belief feels natural and normal to a child.

Christians cite Proverbs 22:6 as a scriptural foundation: “Start children off on the way they should go, and even when they are old they will not turn from it.” This verse is understood as both a promise and a command — parents are responsible for giving their children a foundation of faith from the earliest age. The expectation is not that children will be forced to believe but that early formation creates a path they may choose to walk throughout their lives.

Key Fact

Proverbs 22:6: “Start children off on the way they should go, and even when they are old they will not turn from it.” Christians use this verse to support the practice of raising children within the faith — it implies that early formation shapes character and belief for life. It is the key scriptural anchor for this spec point.

Features of Christian Upbringing and Why They May Lead to Belief

A Christian upbringing works through several interlocking practices. Prayer at home — saying grace before meals, bedtime prayers — models an ongoing relationship with God as natural and routine. Attending church gives the child a community of believers who reinforce Christian identity and demonstrate that faith is practised by real adults they love and respect. Christian festivals — Christmas, Easter, Pentecost — give rhythm and meaning to the year, connecting the child to the story of Jesus from infancy. Faith schools integrate religious teaching across the curriculum and ensure that Christian values shape the whole learning environment.

For many Christians who now hold strong belief as adults, they trace their faith to this kind of early formation. The experience of worshipping, praying and hearing scripture as a child creates deep neural and emotional pathways that can anchor belief through the challenges of adulthood. This is one reason the spec identifies religious upbringing as a potential argument for the existence of God — the fact that millions of people retain Christian belief formed in childhood suggests that early formation transmits something real, not merely cultural habit.

The Challenge: Could Upbringing Lead Away from Belief?

Religious upbringing does not guarantee lifelong belief. Many people raised in Christian households later abandon their faith entirely. They may encounter intellectual challenges (the problem of evil, science and religion) that the faith of their childhood cannot answer, or they may experience hurt or hypocrisy within their church community that erodes trust. This is a genuine counter to the argument that upbringing provides evidence for God: if the belief it produces can be undermined by experience and reflection, perhaps it was never based on truth in the first place — just on socialisation.

Indoctrination is the charge that religious upbringing instils beliefs in children before they are old enough to question or evaluate them. Richard Dawkins argues forcefully in The God Delusion (2006) that there is no such thing as a “Christian child” or a “Muslim child” — only children of Christian or Muslim parents. He contends that describing a child by their parents’ religion and subjecting them to religious education before they can think critically is comparable to any other form of intellectual coercion, and amounts to a form of harm. Humanists similarly argue that children have a right to grow up and reach their own conclusions about religion, and that confessional religious education in faith schools violates this right.

Christians respond to the indoctrination charge on several grounds. First, all upbringings involve values — every family raises its children in particular moral and cultural frameworks, including secular ones. Humanists who raise children with naturalistic assumptions are also forming their children’s worldview before the child is old enough to evaluate it. Second, Christian upbringing at its best does not suppress questioning — good Christian education teaches the reasons for faith and invites honest engagement with doubt. Third, the adult who freely chooses to continue in Christian faith, having had the opportunity to walk away, is not a victim of indoctrination but a person who has made an informed decision. The fact that many people raised in Christian homes later leave the faith shows that the process does not simply produce robots who cannot think; conversely, the fact that many stay shows the faith has genuine staying power.

Key Fact

Dawkins argues in The God Delusion (2006) that labelling children with their parents’ religion before they can evaluate it is a form of harm. Christians respond that all upbringings involve values; that good Christian education invites genuine questioning; and that the adult who freely continues in faith has not been indoctrinated but has made an informed choice.
exam_tip_html: This is a short spec point (3B 1.8) but it generates rich discussion questions. For the 5-mark source answer, Proverbs 22:6 is the named anchor — use the book, chapter and verse. For the 12-mark Discuss, present Dawkins’s indoctrination argument fully (not just in one sentence) and give the Christian responses in equal depth. A common error is to treat religious upbringing as a weak argument and spend most of the 12 marks attacking it — remember to argue both sides with equal development. For the 3-mark Outline question, give three discrete features of Christian upbringing (e.g. baptism, Sunday school, prayer at home) as separate bullet-style points, not one extended answer. SPaG: indoctrination, upbringing, Proverbs.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Proverbs 22:6 (“start children off on the way they should go”) is the scriptural foundation for Christian religious upbringing — early faith formation is seen as a parental responsibility that shapes lifelong belief.
  • Features of a Christian upbringing include prayer, church attendance, baptism, faith schools and Christian festivals — these create an environment in which belief feels natural and may become personally held.
  • Dawkins argues religious upbringing is a form of indoctrination that harms children by instilling beliefs before they can evaluate them critically; Christians respond that all upbringings instil values and that mature faith is freely chosen.

practice_questions.text: Outline three features of a Christian upbringing.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for each of three discrete features: infant baptism or dedication (1); regular church attendance and involvement in the church community (1); prayer at home, including bedtime prayers and saying grace (1). Other valid features include Sunday school, faith schools, Christian festivals. Three distinct points required.

practice_questions.text: Describe Richard Dawkins's argument that religious upbringing is a form of indoctrination.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: Dawkins argues there is no such thing as a 'Christian child' — only a child of Christian parents (1); he argues that labelling children with their parents' religion and teaching it before the child can evaluate it critically is a form of intellectual coercion (1); he claims in The God Delusion (2006) that this amounts to a form of harm to the child (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why Christians believe religious upbringing may lead to genuine belief in God.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per reason (1 for a stated point, 2 for a developed explanation). For example: Regular worship and prayer creates deep emotional and spiritual pathways from childhood that anchor faith through adult challenges, suggesting the belief is genuinely held rather than merely inherited (2); the fact that many adults who were raised as Christians continue in faith after having the opportunity to leave suggests the upbringing transmitted something real about God rather than just cultural habit (2).

practice_questions.text: Explain two Christian reasons for raising children in the faith, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per reason; 1 mark for a named source. Example: Proverbs 22:6 ('Start children off on the way they should go, and even when they are old they will not turn from it') teaches that early formation shapes lifelong character and faith — parents are commanded to provide this foundation (2); Christian community gives the child role models of lived faith, showing that belief is practised by real, trustworthy adults — this embodied witness is more powerful than abstract argument for a young person (2); source credit for Proverbs 22:6 named with chapter and verse (1).

practice_questions.text:
'Religious upbringing is the most important reason why people believe in God.'
Discuss this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; explicit weighing; justified conclusion. Christian case: Proverbs 22:6 supports the practice; upbringing creates genuine, lasting faith; millions of adults with a Christian upbringing freely choose to continue in faith. Counter: Dawkins (The God Delusion, 2006) argues it is indoctrination before critical evaluation; many leave the faith; upbringing-based belief doesn't prove God exists — it only explains why people believe. Evaluate: is upbringing-based belief less 'genuine' than belief reached through argument? Secure (7-9): Both sides present, source named. Developing (4-6): One side dominant. Emerging (1-3): Brief, one-sided. SPaG: indoctrination, upbringing, Proverbs.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why some people argue religious upbringing may lead to a rejection of belief in God, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per reason; 1 mark for a named source. Example: If a child later encounters intellectual challenges to faith (such as the problem of evil) that their upbringing never addressed, they may conclude the beliefs were given without adequate reason and abandon them (2); Dawkins argues in The God Delusion (2006) that children raised in a faith before they can evaluate it critically have been denied the opportunity to reach their own informed conclusions, and some will eventually exercise that right by leaving (2); source credit for Proverbs 22:6 in counter-argument framing, or Dawkins The God Delusion cited explicitly (1).

knowledge_checks.q: What does Proverbs 22:6 say about raising children?
options: Children should choose their own faith when they reach adulthood
Start children off on the way they should go and even when old they will not turn from it
Parents must baptise their children before the age of two
Children who are raised in faith will never face doubt

knowledge_checks.q: What is Richard Dawkins's argument about religious upbringing?
options: Religious upbringing always leads to genuine adult faith
Labelling children with their parents' religion before they can evaluate it critically is a form of harm
Only faith schools provide genuine religious education
Children raised in faith are more likely to become scientists

knowledge_checks.q: Dawkins argues in _____ (2006) that there is no such thing as a 'Christian child' — only a child of Christian parents.
Proverbs 22:6 says to 'start children off on the way they should go' — this is a key Christian basis for _____.
Match each position to its view on religious upbringing:
right: Early faith formation shapes belief for life — a parental responsibility
Labelling children with religion before critical evaluation is a form of harm
All upbringings instil values; adult faith is freely chosen — not indoctrination

flashcard_questions.q: What does Proverbs 22:6 teach about raising children?
flashcard_questions.a: 'Start children off on the way they should go, and even when old they will not turn from it.'

flashcard_questions.q: Name three features of a Christian upbringing.
flashcard_questions.a: Baptism, church attendance, and prayer at home (Sunday school/faith schools also accepted).

flashcard_questions.q: What is the indoctrination argument against religious upbringing?
flashcard_questions.a: Children are taught religious beliefs before they can evaluate them critically — Dawkins calls this a form of harm.

flashcard_questions.q: What did Dawkins say about 'Christian children' in The God Delusion (2006)?
flashcard_questions.a: There is no such thing as a Christian child — only a child of Christian parents who has not yet chosen their own view.

flashcard_questions.q: What is one Christian response to the indoctrination charge?
flashcard_questions.a: All upbringings instil values; the adult who freely continues in faith has made an informed choice, not been indoctrinated.

flashcard_questions.q: Why might religious upbringing sometimes lead to loss of faith?
flashcard_questions.a: Intellectual challenges (e.g. problem of evil) or bad church experiences may undermine beliefs formed in childhood.

flashcard_questions.q: Why do Christians see religious upbringing as an argument for God?
flashcard_questions.a: Millions raised as Christians freely choose to continue in faith as adults, suggesting upbringing transmits something real.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the Humanist view on faith schools?
flashcard_questions.a: Confessional faith education violates children's right to form their own views; all children deserve a neutral secular education.

glossary_terms.definition: Being raised in a faith tradition, including baptism, prayer, church attendance and faith education, which shapes a person's initial beliefs.
An upbringing that includes regular church attendance, Christian prayer, scripture reading, baptism and faith education from birth.
Teaching children beliefs as if they were established facts before the child is old enough to evaluate them critically — used by atheists as a critique of religious upbringing.
A prominent British atheist biologist and author of The God Delusion (2006) who argues that labelling children with their parents' religion is a form of harm.
